newsitem.title: USA: Baseball-Rickey chose Robinson for spiritual reasons.
newsitem.headline: Baseball-Rickey chose Robinson for spiritual reasons.

text.p: It was a far from typical sports anecdote that Brooklyn Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey told in explaining why he chose Jackie Robinson as the right man to break baseball's colour line 50 years ago.

Complete with reference to an old book by an obscure Italian priest, Rickey emphasised Robinson's emotional, intellectual and spiritual strengths as well as his tremendous athletic skills in explaining the decision.

Baseball and President Bill Clinton this Tuesday commemorate the April 15, 1947 date of Robinson's entry to the major leagues, Rickey's "great experiment" which he had planned -- since at least 1942 when he first came to Brooklyn -- with eyes wide open as to its meaning to society at large.

"I believed that the first Negro in professional baseball should have a strong feeling about civil rights because such a person would have a comprehension of the race problem," Rickey wrote in "The American Diamond," published in 1965.
"He could not be the right person and feel only a personal problem."

In their famous first meeting on August 28, 1945, at 215 Montague Street, Brooklyn, the erudite, cigar-smoking, public relations-conscious baseball lifer was impressed with the handsome, well-spoken player's character -- and his anger.

"At the end of a three-hour conference Robinson showed the necessary intelligence and the strength of personality but he had more and deeper racial resentment than was hoped for or expected," Rickey wrote.

The question was, how to use that rage against injustice while keeping it under control in the face of the constant abuse, physical and verbal, Robinson was to face as the first black in modern "organized baseball."

Rickey said the two men, both Methodists, together read a chapter on nonresistance from the book "The Life of Christ" by the Italian priest Giovanni Papini, published in English in 1920 -- 25 years earlier.

"I just happened to have it handy in the top drawer of my desk," Rickey, also known as "The Deacon," wrote. The priest argued that of the possible responses to attack -- revenge, flight or Jesus's "turning of the other cheek" -- the last was actually the most effective.
Heatedly, browbeatingly, Rickey challenged the fiery player to say whether he could hold his temper under the most trying conditions. Robinson promised he would, and history proved he could.
"This was by far the most important point in the hiring of a Negro by a major-league club. Jackie Robinson is Christian by inheritance and practice," wrote Rickey.

"There came the greatness of Jackie Robinson. 'Punch for punch' was, by inheritance, by experience, and by desire, Jackie's quick and natural reaction to insult or attack. To self-impose control of every decent reflex was almost too much to ask for from any man, and particularly from Jackie.

"He was anything (one would think) but ideal for this 'experiment.' It took an intelligent man to understand the challenge -- it took a man of great moral courage to accept it and see it through. He was both."
Of course, the fact that he was a phenomenal athlete didn't hurt, either -- and for that, Rickey had relied on his scouts. Again, history proved the wisdom of the choice.
"There never has been a man in the game who could put mind and muscle together quicker and with better judgment than Robinson," said Rickey, one of baseball's greatest assessors of talent ever.

"Not one could be heard to find serious fault if Robinson were given the second-base position on the all-time All-American club. He was not as great a right-hand batsman as Rogers Hornsby. No one was...

"But he was a skilful batsman with good power. He was a play-maker -- right or left. He could start and/or finish the double play par excellence. He was a fastidious roamer on fly balls -- fair or foul -- all over.
"With a call of two strikes, no man living, then or now, could threaten a pitcher with more imminent disaster.
"On the base paths he could turn a ball game around. He was a student of pitchers' moves and an instant learner of them -- a master of commanding leads and making the daring 'break.'"
Rickey noted that Robinson in his prime years "batted fourth but if leading off could bunt."

Also, Robinson's bravery in the face of the abuse he faced brought his teammates together -- even the Southerners who had drawn up a petition to bar him. That "built a surprising fight and stick-to-itiveness in team morale that lifted a club from that time into pennant comtention."
Summarized Rickey: "Robinson was better under pressure."
